info.bio:
Black Flag es una banda de hardcore punk formada en 1977 en Hermosa Beach, California. El grupo fue idea original de Greg Ginn, guitarrista, principal compositor y único miembro actual tras muchos cambios que tuvo la banda a lo largo de su corta historia. Son considerados como una de las bandas mas influyentes que dieron lugar al hardcore punk, junto con agrupaciones como Bad Brains y Minor threat.

Black Flag creó un sonido único a partir de mezclar la simpleza en bruto de los míticos Ramones, con tonos más agudos y velocidades rápidas.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk como «violento, rápido y ruidoso» tarda en conquistar EE UU, pero cuando lo hace el hardcore se convierte durante dos décadas en el idioma nacional de millones de chavales. Misfits y el «scum-rock»; el crossover punk-metal (Suicidal Tendencies, Corrosion Of Conformity, Agnostic Front); Mission Of Burma en Boston. Washington: Bad Brains (reggae, funk y metal diez años por delante), Minor Threat (el «straight-edge») y Rites Of Spring, inventores del emo-core. San Francisco: Dead Kennedys de Jello Biafra, D.R.I. (thrash antes que Metallica), Flipper. Los «beach punks» de Los Ángeles: Germs, X, Black Flag (Damaged), Descendents, Gun Club (Fire Of Love), Bad Religion. El jazz-core de Minutemen y Saccharine Trust; en el Medio Oeste, Husker Du y Replacements cambian el hardcore para siempre; en Chicago, Naked Raygun y Big Black de Steve Albini; en Europa, The Ex y los italianos CCCP.

podcast.title: Fidget Spinners as Merch (2017)
podcast.body: Black Flag, among numerous other bands and artists, sold branded fidget spinners as merchandise in 2017. This reflects a trend where fidget spinners became one of the top-selling band merch items for the year. "Everybody sold branded fidget spinners, arcade fire, David Bowie, Prince Black Flag, the misfits, Nirvana, Queens of the Stone Age, followed boy, weird."

podcast.title: Association with Slam Dancing
podcast.body: Black Flag is mentioned in the context of Orange County punks who popularized slam dancing in the late 1970s. Their performances at clubs like The Cuckoo's Nest are cited as part of the birth of this aggressive dance style. "Black flag, fear, bands like that. Playing at clubs like The Cookus Nest in Costa Mesa, which has gone down on history as the birthplace of slam dancing."

podcast.title: Formation of SST Records
podcast.body: In a true demonstration of the "do-it-yourself" ethos, Black Flag decided to form their own record label, SST Records, when no major label would sign them. The label was named after an old electronic company and was initially managed directly by the band's guitarist, bassist, and two roadies. "So in true, do it yourself, Sphere, the flag formed their own record label."

podcast.title: Henry Rollins – Former 7-Eleven Clerk from DC Replaced Co-Founder, Took Band to New Level
podcast.body: Black Flag was co-founded in 1976 with Keith Morris as singer, but Morris was gone by 1979 (creative differences, cocaine and speed). After brief stints by Ron Reyes and Dez Cadena, the band discovered Henry Rollins — a Washington, D.C. hardcore fan and former 7-Eleven clerk — who had attended their shows. Rollins took Black Flag to an entirely new level and remained their singer until they broke up in summer 1986. "His replacement was a former 7-11 clerk from Washington, D.C., named Henry Rollins."

podcast.title: Independent Label Founding (SST)
podcast.body: When no one would release their record, founder Greg Ginn and bass player Chuck Dukowski formed SST, an independent record label. The label's name is an abbreviation for Solid State Tuners, which was Greg Ginn's side business selling ham radio electronics by mail. "When the group couldn't get anyone to put out the record, Greg and bass player Chuck Dukowski formed SST, which is short for Solid State Tuners."

podcast.body: Black Flag's hardcore punk tracks were included on cassettes distributed by Buzz Osborne in Aberdeen, Washington, influencing the emerging Seattle sound. In Seattle, it was not considered strange to be a fan of both Black Flag and Aerosmith simultaneously, leading to a unique hybrid sound. "Hardcore punk mixed easily with hard rock and Seattle. podcast.title: Lack of Major Label Interest
podcast.body: Despite being recognized as one of the best underground groups in Southern California in the early 1980s, Black Flag struggled to secure a record deal. Major labels on the West Coast, operating under the conventional wisdom that punk was a passing fad, were unwilling to take a risk on signing a punk band. "Although the flag were clearly one of the best underground groups in all of Southern California, there wasn't a single record label willing to risk signing them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Most Important American Indie Act
podcast.body: Black Flag became one of the most important American indie acts of all time, especially after Henry Rollins from Washington D.C. joined as their vocalist. The band's inability to find an existing record label willing to release their music led their guitarist, Greg Ginn, to transform his electronics company into SST Records to distribute their work. "Flag became one of the most important American index of all time, especially after a kid from Washington D.C. named Henry Rollins joined in his vocalist."

podcast.title: Road Incident with Mugger
podcast.body: On the way to a gig in San Diego, while stuck in a traffic jam, Black Flag's van was cut off by a woman driving a large car. Mugger, a member of the entourage, was so frustrated that he hopped out of the van and dumped his yogurt through her car window. This led to the band being "busted," with Greg having to handle the conversation with the authorities to resolve the incident. "Mugger had had enough of her bolt-ish and hopped out of the van and dumped his yogurt through her window."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spreading Hardcore Gospel
podcast.body: Black Flag was noted for spreading the "gospel of hardcore" through constant touring. Their music was also part of the "unique stew of influences" that shaped the Seattle sound, where it was not considered strange to be into both hardcore punk and traditional hard rock simultaneously. "And there were bands like Black Flag and Bad Religion that spread the gospel of hardcore by touring constantly. ...No one considered it weird to be into both Black Flag and Arasmith at the same time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stage Attack in San Diego
podcast.body: During a show in San Diego, Henry Rollins was attacked on stage by a woman and her boyfriend, along with two friends, who were reportedly under the influence of Angel Dust. Rollins was dragged off stage and repeatedly hit in the face. The attacker was eventually pulled off, and Rollins finished the set before going to the men's room to straighten out his nose, which ended up slightly crooked. "Play the first few songs and see the squirrel trying to grab me. I move away from her. Her boyfriend and his two friends are apparently on Angel Dust and see this as a great opportunity to drag me off stage and beat this shit out of me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Struggles and Legal Battles
podcast.body: Black Flag endured several years of struggle and financial difficulty. They nearly lost a significant legal battle with a major label, an event that could have potentially ended both the band and their newly formed independent label. Despite these obstacles, they eventually mastered the complexities of running an independent company and achieved considerable success. "Black Flag struggled for a few years, almost losing a legal battle with a major label that would have killed both the band and their label, but eventually they got the hang of running an independent company and did quite well."

xref.title: Black Flag's "Damaged" as a Revelation
xref.body: Nate Mendel's understanding of hardcore punk solidified upon listening to Black Flag's "Damaged" album. He initially didn't grasp it, but halfway through, "it clicked," revealing to him the energy, aggression, and "weirdness" of the genre that he came to love. "Well, the one that, that, where I understood what hardcore we call it, hardcore at the time was about, was, uh, black flags damaged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: California Hardcore Scene
xref.body: The Offspring were deeply rooted in the California hardcore scene, a fierce but small community dedicated to punk that evolved from the original 1970s punk. This music became a soundtrack for skaters and snowboarders, including bands like Dead Kennedys, The Adolescents, The Vandals, Black Flag, and Bad Religion, which was niche and rarely played on radio. "Everyone was into California hardcore. The punk that evolved out of the original punk of the 1970s. The scene was small but fierce and its adherents stuck together. And some of this music became the soundtrack for skaters and snowboarders, dead candidates, the adolescence, the vandals, black flag, bad religion, really niche stuff at the time, and certainly stuff that never made it on the radio."

xref.title: Cassette Distributor
xref.body: A young musician from Aberdeen, Washington, Buzz Osborne was known for distributing homemade cassettes featuring his favorite punk songs, including tracks from indie bands, The Stooges, Bad Brains, and Black Flag, only to people he deemed "cool." These tapes are credited with changing the world of rock and roll forever. "Several years earlier, a young musician from the logging town of Aberdeen, Washington, named Buzz Osborne began giving out cassettes featuring his favorite punk songs, All Indie bands, TBI from the stuages, tracks from bad brains and black flag, and Buzz gave these tapes only to people he considered cool."

xref.title: Early Distribution Struggles
xref.body: Bad Religion, a Southern California punk band, faced similar challenges as Black Flag in the early 1980s, unable to find anyone willing to distribute their self-produced records. This led the band to take a do-it-yourself approach to ensure their music reached an audience. "They also couldn't find anyone willing to distribute their self-produced records."

xref.title: Early Musical Education – Self-Taught with Records and Pillows
xref.body: Dave Grohl grew up in Washington D.C., where he learned to play drums and guitar by meticulously studying records from bands like KISS, Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, Black Flag, The Stooges, and Motorhead. While he took guitar lessons first, he taught himself drums by arranging pillows on his bed and practicing with borrowed sticks. "he learned the drums by arranging pillows on his bed and banging them with some borrowed sticks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Self-Tattoo Attempt (Age 12-13)
xref.body: Inspired by a scene in the movie "Christian F." where a character gives herself a stick-and-poke tattoo, Dave Grohl attempted to give himself a Black Flag tattoo on his forearm at the age of 12 or 13. He used a needle and thread from his mother's sewing kit and managed about a third of the thick black design before stopping due to pain, and still retains the "crappy tattoo." "When I saw that, I was like, I can do this myself. So I went to my mother's sewing kit and I got some thread and I got the needle. And I found something and I started giving myself a black flag tattoo. I think I was 12 or 13 years old on my forearm."

xref.title: Founding Alternative Tentacles
xref.body: The Dead Kennedys formed Alternative Tentacles, a California label, initially just to release one of their singles. They enjoyed the experience so much they decided to turn it into a full-time business, following the model of Black Flag with SST and Bad Religion with Epitaph. The label also played a key role in exporting American hardcore by developing relationships with other indie labels worldwide. "At first, they just wanted to get one of their singles out there, but they enjoyed the experience so much that they decided to turn Alternative Tentacles into a full-time business..."

xref.body: Bad Religion, like Black Flag, faced the challenge of no one wanting to release their music. This compelled them to establish their own label, Epitaph, which initially served as a platform solely for their own records but later grew significantly beyond hardcore punk. "Another band that found themselves in the same boat as Black Flag was Bad Religion. No one wanted to release their stuff either, so they had to establish their own label, and they called theirs Epitaph."

xref.body: A deal with Black Flag's SST Records enabled Sonic Youth to significantly expand their influence across North America. This collaboration was crucial for their reach in the independent music scene. "And thanks to a deal with Black Flag's SSD records, they were able to spread their influence throughout North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Spreading Hardcore Gospel
xref.body: Bad Religion, alongside Black Flag, was instrumental in disseminating the "gospel of hardcore" through their consistent touring efforts. "And there were bands like Black Flag and Bad Religion that spread the gospel of hardcore by touring constantly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Major Label
xref.body: After releasing several records, some on Black Flag's SST label, Hüsker Dü signed with a major label, Warner, while managing to retain complete creative control over their music. "Hustler Doe found a lot of love on college radio, and after a series of records, some of which Ron Blackflegs' SST label, they were signed, my god, to a major record label, Warner scooped them up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
